phase: blind lock before raw capture, unblind mapping, authored keys or explanations

supported_choice_texts: The lists of required materials, including textbooks, lab goggles, and a scientific calculator, are available at the bookstore.
The list of required materials, including textbooks, lab goggles, and a scientific calculator, is available at the bookstore.
rows.proof: Both plural lists/are and singular list/is correct the agreement error. The stem permits a revision and does not require preserving the subject number or replacing only the verb. They are different propositions, not equivalent options.

supported_choice_texts: The lists of required materials, including scissors, glue, and colored paper, are on the teacher's desk.
The list of required materials, including scissors, glue, and colored paper, is on the teacher's desk.
rows.proof: Both lists/are and list/is agree. No rule in the visible revision task prevents changing the subject number.

supported_choice_texts: Neither the coach nor the players were satisfied with the referee's decision.
rows.proof: Plural nearer subject players takes were. Has is singular; the coaches/player version has singular nearer player with were; neither/or is not the stated standard correlative form.

supported_choice_texts: Maya told Priya that Maya's presentation needed more data.
rows.proof: Only the explicit name Maya fixes the owner. Her own can still refer to Maya or Priya; she remains ambiguous. Their can refer to a shared group or to an individual under singular they, so it does not unequivocally identify one owner. No original intended owner needs to be inferred to recognize that the explicit-name revision removes this ambiguity.

supported_choice_texts: finished
rows.proof: The stem explicitly requires simple past for a completed event: finished. The other choices are present singular, present perfect or future.

supported_choice_texts: is
rows.proof: The subject head list is singular, so is agrees. Are/were are plural and be is not the finite indicative form in this sentence. Offering the unchanged correct form is consistent with the requested replacement.

supported_choice_texts: is
rows.proof: The singular head list takes is, regardless of the plural materials inside the modifying phrase. The alternatives do not supply the required finite singular form.

supported_choice_texts: Elena
Maria
rows.proof: Both Elena and Maria identify a specific person and remove the ambiguous she. The stem does not state which person must remain the intended referent. Multiple answers exist even without considering the role-noun alternatives.

supported_choice_texts: have
rows.proof: The nearer subject players is plural, so have decided is the agreeing present-perfect form. Has/is are singular; are having decided is not the corresponding grammatical finite construction.

supported_choice_texts: By the time the meeting starts, the committee will have already voted on the proposal.
rows.proof: Will have already voted is the conventional future-completion correction. However, the unrestricted revision task also changes the time clause in an offered past-framing answer and gives no explicit tense/aspect preservation instruction. The acceptability of the offered simple-past already version in formal written English is uncertain; do not silently enforce a future-perfect-only task.
uncertainty: D: past framing; A/C also change aspect or habitual framing and need interpretation.

supported_choice_texts: Maria told Elena that Maria's presentation needed more data.
rows.proof: The explicit name Maria resolves ownership. Independently, choices B and C differ only by optional complementizer that and express the same ambiguous she/her revision, so two wrong alternatives duplicate one another.

supported_choice_texts: had finished
rows.proof: Had finished explicitly marks prior completion. Finished with by the time can also receive a completed-before-past-event reading when chronology is clear. The question describes temporal meaning rather than explicitly requesting the past-perfect form; past-perfect versus simple-past necessity remains uncertain. No universal past-perfect-only rule is assumed.
uncertainty: C: finished may also fit the stated completed-before relationship.

supported_choice_texts: has
rows.proof: Each is singular; has submitted agrees. Have is plural and were/are submitted does not agree with the singular subject or express the same completed submission.

supported_choice_texts: By the time the meeting starts, the committee will have already voted on the proposal.
rows.proof: Will have already voted is the expected future-perfect correction. The stem asks for a revision without specifying completed-future meaning or permitted span. Other offered present/ongoing versions change aspect rather than simply guaranteeing the original completion; uniqueness cannot be established without interpreting an unstated intended revision constraint.
uncertainty: A/C: habitual or ongoing readings versus intended future completion.

supported_choice_texts: the intern's
the manager's
rows.proof: Both the interns computer and the managers computer make ownership explicit. Nothing in the prompt selects one intended owner.

supported_choice_texts: When the manager met with the intern, the former asked several questions about the budget.
When the manager met with the intern, the manager asked several questions about the budget.
rows.proof: Former refers to the first of manager/intern, the manager. A and C therefore identify the same speaker and are equivalent correct revisions. One of them and he himself remain ambiguous.

supported_choice_texts: When the manager spoke to the intern, the manager seemed frustrated.
rows.proof: The explicit manager uniquely identifies who seemed frustrated. The other versions retain ambiguous he and sometimes add another ambiguous pronoun. Different added clauses produce distinct alternative revisions.

supported_choice_texts: the coach
the captain
rows.proof: Both the coach and the captain replace they with an explicit person. The task supplies no intended referent; at least those two answers are correct regardless of the other nouns.

supported_choice_texts: Neither the coaches nor the player was ready to leave the field after the loss.
Neither the coach nor the players were ready to leave the field after the loss.
rows.proof: Both coaches/nor/player/was and coach/nor/players/were follow agreement with the nearer noun. The task does not restrict changing participant number, so both revisions correct agreement.

supported_choice_texts: the laptop
the concrete floor
rows.proof: Both the laptop and the concrete floor are explicit plausible objects that might be undamaged. The stem does not specify which object the pronoun must refer to.

method: Manual literal-task assessment of each original stem and all offered alternatives. Treatment/call labels remain hidden. A defect may be definite multiple answers/equivalence or separately recorded uncertainty. No implied task is supplied to rescue an item.
prior_visibility: Aggregate transport/status/usage only. Another reviewer reported aggregate7 supported, but no item-level results or arm allocation were opened. These judgments were determined independently; root finds8 supported.

grammar_sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Martin Hewings, Advanced Grammar in Use, Unit5 (publisher excerpt mirror), page10/PDF13
grammar_sources.use: The rule allows past simple or perfect in some contexts with clearly established event order; it does not establish that every earlier event requires past perfect. Application to these exact offered sentences remains explicitly uncertain.

grammar_sources.title: Oxford Advanced Learners Dictionary: already
grammar_sources.use: North American simple-past usage with already exists, but the entry qualifies formal written acceptability and recommends past perfect in past context. This supports caution rather than a blanket acceptance of the offered past-framing revision.
